claim: Pannexins are large-pore forming channels responsible for ATP release under a variety of physiological and pathological conditions.
source: Pannexins are large-pore forming channels responsible for ATP release under a variety of physiological and pathological conditions.
evidence: This is a general statement about pannexin function that is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations in the manuscript.

claim: Pannexins have minimal sequence similarity to connexins, innexins, and LRRC8.
source: Although predicted to share similar membrane topology with other large-pore forming proteins such as connexins, innexins, and LRRC8, pannexins have minimal sequence similarity to these protein families.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by sequence analysis knowledge.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of frog pannexin 1 (Panx1) channel was determined at 3.0 Å resolution.
source: Here, we present the cryo-EM structure of a frog pannexin 1 (Panx1) channel at 3.0 Å.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Panx1 protomers harbor four transmembrane helices.
source: We find that Panx1 protomers harbor four transmembrane helices similar in arrangement to other large-pore forming proteins but assemble as a heptameric channel with a unique constriction formed by Trp74 in the first extracellular loop.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and shown in structural figures.

claim: Panx1 assembles as a heptameric channel.
source: We find that Panx1 protomers harbor four transmembrane helices similar in arrangement to other large-pore forming proteins but assemble as a heptameric channel with a unique constriction formed by Trp74 in the first extracellular loop.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by cryo-EM structural data.

claim: Panx1 has a unique constriction formed by Trp74 in the first extracellular loop.
source: We find that Panx1 protomers harbor four transmembrane helices similar in arrangement to other large-pore forming proteins but assemble as a heptameric channel with a unique constriction formed by Trp74 in the first extracellular loop.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and shown in structural analysis.

claim: Mutating Trp74 or the nearby Arg75 disrupts ion selectivity.
source: Mutating Trp74 or the nearby Arg75 disrupt ion selectivity, whereas altering residues in the hydrophobic groove formed by the two extracellular loops abrogates channel inhibition by carbenoxolone.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 3.

claim: Altering residues in the hydrophobic groove formed by the two extracellular loops abrogates channel inhibition by carbenoxolone.
source: Mutating Trp74 or the nearby Arg75 disrupt ion selectivity, whereas altering residues in the hydrophobic groove formed by the two extracellular loops abrogates channel inhibition by carbenoxolone.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: The extracellular loops are important structural motifs for ion selectivity and channel inhibition in Panx1.
source: Our structural and functional study establishes the extracellular loops as important structural motifs for ion selectivity and channel inhibition in Panx1.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, supported by structural and functional data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Pannexins regulate nucleotide release during apoptosis.
source: Pannexins are a family of ubiquitously expressed large-pore forming channels which regulate nucleotide release during apoptosis (Chekeni et al., 2010), blood pressure (Billaud et al., 2011; Billaud et al., 2015), and neuropathic pain (Bravo et al., 2014; Weaver et al., 2017; Mousseau et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Pannexins regulate blood pressure.
source: Pannexins are a family of ubiquitously expressed large-pore forming channels which regulate nucleotide release during apoptosis (Chekeni et al., 2010), blood pressure (Billaud et al., 2011; Billaud et al., 2015), and neuropathic pain (Bravo et al., 2014; Weaver et al., 2017; Mousseau et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Pannexins regulate neuropathic pain.
source: Pannexins are a family of ubiquitously expressed large-pore forming channels which regulate nucleotide release during apoptosis (Chekeni et al., 2010), blood pressure (Billaud et al., 2011; Billaud et al., 2015), and neuropathic pain (Bravo et al., 2014; Weaver et al., 2017; Mousseau et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Pannexins have limited sequence identity with innexins (~15% identity).
source: While pannexins have limited sequence identity with innexins (~15% identity), they have virtually no sequence similarity to other large-pore forming channels (Panchin et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Pannexins have virtually no sequence similarity to other large-pore forming channels.
source: While pannexins have limited sequence identity with innexins (~15% identity), they have virtually no sequence similarity to other large-pore forming channels (Panchin et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Panx1 is a large-pore forming channel responsible for ATP release from a variety of cell types.
source: Among the pannexin family, pannexin 1 (Panx1) has garnered the most attention for its role as a large-pore forming channel responsible for ATP release from a variety of cell types (Bao et al., 2004; Dahl, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Voltage activates Panx1.
source: Different kinds of stimuli have been reported to activate Panx1 including voltage, membrane stretch, increased intracellular calcium levels, and positive membrane potentials (Bruzzone et al., 2003; Bao et al., 2004; Locovei et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2014; Chiu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Membrane stretch activates Panx1.
source: Different kinds of stimuli have been reported to activate Panx1 including voltage, membrane stretch, increased intracellular calcium levels, and positive membrane potentials (Bruzzone et al., 2003; Bao et al., 2004; Locovei et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2014; Chiu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Increased intracellular calcium levels activate Panx1.
source: Different kinds of stimuli have been reported to activate Panx1 including voltage, membrane stretch, increased intracellular calcium levels, and positive membrane potentials (Bruzzone et al., 2003; Bao et al., 2004; Locovei et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2014; Chiu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Positive membrane potentials activate Panx1.
source: Different kinds of stimuli have been reported to activate Panx1 including voltage, membrane stretch, increased intracellular calcium levels, and positive membrane potentials (Bruzzone et al., 2003; Bao et al., 2004; Locovei et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2014; Chiu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Proteases can permanently or temporarily stimulate Panx1 channel activity.
source: Panx1 is also targeted by signaling effectors, such as proteases and kinases, to permanently or temporarily stimulate channel activity (Pelegrin and Surprenant, 2006; Thompson et al., 2008; Sandilos et al., 2012; Billaud et al., 2015; Lohman et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Kinases can permanently or temporarily stimulate Panx1 channel activity.
source: Panx1 is also targeted by signaling effectors, such as proteases and kinases, to permanently or temporarily stimulate channel activity (Pelegrin and Surprenant, 2006; Thompson et al., 2008; Sandilos et al., 2012; Billaud et al., 2015; Lohman et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Panx1 has a capacity to integrate distinct stimuli into channel activation leading to ATP release.
source: The above evidence suggests that Panx1 has a capacity to integrate distinct stimuli into channel activation leading to ATP release.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited evidence in the introduction.

claim: Frog Panx1 (frPanx1) is 66% identical to human Panx1.
source: Frog Panx1 (frPanx1; 66% identical to human, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) displayed high expression levels and remained monodisperse when solubilized in detergent, suggesting high biochemical integrity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by sequence alignment data.

claim: Frog Panx1 displayed high expression levels and remained monodisperse when solubilized in detergent.
source: Frog Panx1 (frPanx1; 66% identical to human, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) displayed high expression levels and remained monodisperse when solubilized in detergent, suggesting high biochemical integrity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by FSEC data.

claim: frPanx1 was stabilized by truncating the C-terminus by 71 amino acids and by removing 24 amino acids from the intracellular loop between transmembrane helices 2 and 3.
source: We further stabilized frPanx1 by truncating the C-terminus by 71 amino acids and by removing 24 amino acids from the intracellular loop between transmembrane helices 2 and 3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and describes the experimental approach.

claim: frPanx1-ΔLC displayed high stability in detergents and could be purified to homogeneity.
source: This construct, dubbed 'frPanx1-ΔLC', displayed high stability in detergents and could be purified to homogeneity (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a and b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by chromatography and gel data.

claim: frPanx1 forms a functional pannexin channel.
source: We verified that frPanx1 forms a functional pannexin channel by whole-cell patch clamp electrophysiology (Figure 1a and b; Figure 1—figure supplement 2e and f).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by electrophysiology data.

claim: A total of 90,185 selected particles were used for 3D reconstruction at 3.0 Å resolution.
source: We used a total of 90,185 selected particles for 3D reconstruction at 3.0 Å resolution (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and describes the cryo-EM data processing.

claim: The map quality was sufficient for de novo model building for the majority of frPanx1-ΔLC with the exception of disordered segments of the N-terminus (residues 1–10), ECL1 (88–100), and ICL1 (157–194).
source: The map quality was sufficient for de novo model building for the majority of frPanx1-ΔLC with the exception of disordered segments of the N-terminus (residues 1–10), ECL1 (88–100), and ICL1 (157–194) (Figure 1c; Figure 1—figure supplement 4, Video 1, and Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and describes the quality of the cryo-EM map.

claim: The heptameric assembly of Panx1 is unique among known eukaryotic channels.
source: The frPanx1-ΔLC structure revealed a heptameric assembly, which is unique among the known eukaryotic channels (Figure 1d and e).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural comparison with other channels.

claim: Connexins are hexameric.
source: Other large-pore forming channels include hexameric connexins (Maeda et al., 2009) and LRRC8s (Deneka et al., 2018; Kasuya et al., 2018; Kefauver et al., 2018), and the octameric innexins (Oshima et al., 2016) and calcium homeostasis modulator1 (CALHM1) (Syrjanen et al., 2020; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: LRRC8s are hexameric.
source: Other large-pore forming channels include hexameric connexins (Maeda et al., 2009) and LRRC8s (Deneka et al., 2018; Kasuya et al., 2018; Kefauver et al., 2018), and the octameric innexins (Oshima et al., 2016) and calcium homeostasis modulator1 (CALHM1) (Syrjanen et al., 2020; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: Innexins are octameric.
source: Other large-pore forming channels include hexameric connexins (Maeda et al., 2009) and LRRC8s (Deneka et al., 2018; Kasuya et al., 2018; Kefauver et al., 2018), and the octameric innexins (Oshima et al., 2016) and calcium homeostasis modulator1 (CALHM1) (Syrjanen et al., 2020; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: CALHM1 is octameric.
source: Other large-pore forming channels include hexameric connexins (Maeda et al., 2009) and LRRC8s (Deneka et al., 2018; Kasuya et al., 2018; Kefauver et al., 2018), and the octameric innexins (Oshima et al., 2016) and calcium homeostasis modulator1 (CALHM1) (Syrjanen et al., 2020; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: Previous studies suggested hexameric assembly of pannexin based on single channel recordings on concatemeric channels and negative stain electron microscopy.
source: Our result differs from previous studies that suggest hexameric assembly of pannexin based on single channel recordings on concatemeric channels and negative stain electron microscopy (Boassa et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2014; Chiu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The heptameric assembly observed in the current study is unlikely to be caused by the carboxy-terminal truncation or intracellular loop deletion.
source: The heptameric assembly observed in the current study is unlikely to be caused by the carboxy-terminal truncation or intracellular loop deletion because cryo-EM images of the full-length frPanx1 also display clear seven-fold symmetry in the 2D class averages (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by cryo-EM data of full-length protein.

claim: 2D class averages of hPanx1 display a heptameric assembly.
source: Furthermore, 2D class averages of hPanx1 display a heptameric assembly, but not other oligomeric states (Figure 2—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by cryo-EM data.

claim: The major oligomeric state of Panx1 is a heptamer.
source: Thus, overall, our data suggests that the major oligomeric state of Panx1 is a heptamer.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: The heptameric assembly is established by inter-subunit interactions at three locations: 1) ECL1s and the loop between β2 and β3; 2) TM1-TM1 and TM2-TM4 interfaces; and 3) α9 helix and the surrounding α3 and α4 helices, and the N-terminal loop from the neighboring subunit.
source: This unique heptameric assembly is established by inter-subunit interactions at three locations: 1) ECL1s and the loop between β2 and β3; 2) TM1-TM1 and TM2-TM4 interfaces; and 3) α9 helix and the surrounding α3 and α4 helices, and the N-terminal loop from the neighboring subunit (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural analysis.

claim: The majority of residues mediating inter-subunit interactions are highly conserved (e.g. Phe67 and Tyr111).
source: Notably, the majority of residues mediating these interactions are highly conserved (e.g. Phe67 and Tyr111; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by sequence alignment data.

claim: The overall protomer structure of Panx1 resembles that of other large-pore forming channels including connexin, innexins, and LRRC8.
source: The overall protomer structure of Panx1 resembles that of other large-pore forming channels including connexin, innexins, and LRRC8.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural comparison.

claim: Each Panx1 protomer harbors four transmembrane helices (TM1-4), two extracellular loops (ECL1 and 2), two intracellular loops (ICL1 and 2), and an amino (N)-terminal loop.
source: Like other large-pore forming channels, each Panx1 protomer harbors four transmembrane helices (TM1-4), two extracellular loops (ECL1 and 2), two intracellular loops (ICL1 and 2), and an amino (N)-terminal loop (Figure 2a and b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in structural figures.

claim: The transmembrane helices of Panx1 are assembled as a bundle in which the overall helix lengths, angles, and positions strongly resemble the transmembrane arrangements observed in other large-pore channels.
source: The transmembrane helices of Panx1 are assembled as a bundle in which the overall helix lengths, angles, and positions strongly resemble the transmembrane arrangements observed in other large-pore channels (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural comparison.

claim: Panx1 has no similarity in transmembrane arrangement to CALHMs.
source: In contrast, Panx1 has no similarity in transmembrane arrangement to another group of large-pore channels, CALHMs whose protomers also contain four transmembrane helices (Choi et al., 2019; Syrjanen et al., 2020; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural comparison and citations.

claim: Structural features in the Panx1 ECL1 and ECL2 domains are conserved among large-pore channels despite limited sequence similarity.
source: Structural features in the Panx1 ECL1 and ECL2 domains are conserved among large-pore channels despite limited sequence similarity (Figure 2d–g; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural comparison.

claim: The Panx1 ECL1 and ECL2 are joined together by two conserved disulfide bonds (Cys66 with Cys267, Cys84 with Cys248).
source: For example, the Panx1 ECL1 and ECL2 are joined together by two conserved disulfide bonds (Cys66 with Cys267, Cys84 with Cys248) in addition to several β-strands.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: ECL1 contains an alpha-helix that extends towards the central pore and forms an extracellular constriction of the permeation pathway.
source: ECL1 also contains an alpha-helix that extends towards the central pore and forms an extracellular constriction of the permeation pathway.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The Panx1 intracellular domains are structurally unique.
source: While much of the transmembrane domains and extracellular loops show similarities to other large-pore forming channels, the Panx1 intracellular domains are structurally unique (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural comparison.

claim: ICL1 and ICL2 together form a bundle of helices that make contact with the N-terminus.
source: ICL1 and ICL2, for example, together form a bundle of helices that make contact with the N-terminus.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The N-terminal loop of Panx1 forms a constriction of the permeation pathway and extends towards the intracellular region.
source: The N-terminal loop of Panx1 forms a constriction of the permeation pathway and extends towards the intracellular region.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The first ~10 amino acids of the N-terminus are disordered in the structure.
source: The first ~10 amino acids of the N-terminus are disordered in our structure, but these residues might play a role in ion permeation or ion selectivity (Wang and Dahl, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The first ~10 amino acids of the N-terminus might play a role in ion permeation or ion selectivity.
source: The first ~10 amino acids of the N-terminus are disordered in our structure, but these residues might play a role in ion permeation or ion selectivity (Wang and Dahl, 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation.

claim: The Panx1 permeation pathway spans a length of 104 Å.
source: The Panx1 permeation pathway spans a length of 104 Å, with constrictions formed by the N-terminal loop, Ile58, and Trp74 (Figure 3a and b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural analysis.

claim: The Panx1 permeation pathway has constrictions formed by the N-terminal loop, Ile58, and Trp74.
source: The Panx1 permeation pathway spans a length of 104 Å, with constrictions formed by the N-terminal loop, Ile58, and Trp74 (Figure 3a and b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural analysis.

claim: The narrowest constriction is surrounded by Trp74 located on ECL1.
source: The narrowest constriction is surrounded by Trp74 located on ECL1 (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: Trp74 is highly conserved among species including hPanx1.
source: Trp74 is highly conserved among species including hPanx1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by sequence alignment data.

claim: Panx1 has been previously characterized as an anion selective channel.
source: Because Panx1 has been previously characterized as an anion selective channel (Ma et al., 2012; Romanov et al., 2012; Chiu et al., 2014), we wondered if positively charged amino acids around the narrowest constriction formed by Trp74 may contribute to anion selectivity of the channel.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: Arg75 is situated nearest to the tightest constriction of the permeation pathway.
source: Interestingly, Arg75 is situated nearest to the tightest constriction of the permeation pathway (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: Arg75 might be a major determinant of anion selectivity of Panx1 channels in the open state.
source: We hypothesized that Arg75 might be a major determinant of anion selectivity of Panx1 channels in the open state.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the Results section.

claim: When treated with gluconate, the reversal potential of wild-type Panx1 shifted to +26 mV, suggesting the channel is more permeable to Cl- than to Gluc-.
source: When treated with the large anion, gluconate (Gluc-), Erev shifted to +26 mV, suggesting the channel is more permeable to Cl- than to Gluc-.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by electrophysiology data.

claim: When exposed to NMDG+, the reversal potential of wild-type Panx1 remained close to 0 mV, suggesting that Na+ and NMDG+ equally (or do not) permeate Panx1.
source: When exposed to the large cation, N-methyl-D-glucamine (NMDG+), Erev remained close to 0 mV, suggesting that Na+ and NMDG+ equally (or do not) permeate Panx1.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by electrophysiology data.

claim: The Arg75Lys mutant maintains the positive charge at position 75 and displayed Erev values comparable to WT.
source: The Arg75Lys mutant maintains the positive charge of this position, and displayed Erev values comparable to WT.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by electrophysiology data.

claim: The Arg75Ala mutant diminished Cl- selectivity.
source: Removing the positive charge at this position, as shown by the Arg75Ala mutant, diminished Cl- selectivity as the Erev in NaGluc remained near 0 mV.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by electrophysiology data.

claim: The Arg75Ala mutant lost anion selectivity and Na+ became more permeable than NMDG+.
source: Interestingly, the Erev in NMDGCl shifted to −22 mV, suggesting the channel had lost anion selectivity and Na+ became more permeable than NMDG+.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by electrophysiology data.

claim: The Arg75Glu mutant shifted the Erev in NaGluc to −16 mV and in NMDGCl to −45 mV, indicating that Gluc- became more permeable to Cl-.
source: A charge reversal mutant, Arg75Glu, shifted the Erev in NaGluc to −16 mV and in NMDGCl to −45 mV, indicating that Gluc- became more permeable to Cl-.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by electrophysiology data.

claim: The positively charged Arg75 plays a role in anion selectivity of Panx1.
source: Overall, these results support the idea that the positively charged Arg75 plays a role in anion selectivity of Panx1.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on mutagenesis data.

claim: Both Trp74Arg and Trp74Glu mutants become less selective to anions and more permeable to Na+.
source: Interestingly, both Trp74Arg and Trp74Glu mutants become less selective to anions and more permeable to Na+ (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by electrophysiology data.

claim: Introducing a charge at position 74 disrupts the natural ion selectivity of Panx1 channels but position 74 itself does not control ion selectivity.
source: These results suggest that introducing a charge at this position disrupts the natural ion selectivity of Panx1 channels but that position 74 itself does not control ion selectivity.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the Results section based on mutagenesis data.

claim: The distance between the guanidino group of Arg75 and the benzene ring of Trp74 from an adjacent subunit is ~4 Å.
source: We observed that the distance between the guanidino group of Arg75 and the benzene ring of Trp74 from an adjacent subunit is ~4 Å, suggesting that these two residues likely participate in an inter-subunit cation-π interaction key to Panx1 ion selectivity (Figure 3f).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data.

claim: Trp74 and Arg75 likely participate in an inter-subunit cation-π interaction key to Panx1 ion selectivity.
source: We observed that the distance between the guanidino group of Arg75 and the benzene ring of Trp74 from an adjacent subunit is ~4 Å, suggesting that these two residues likely participate in an inter-subunit cation-π interaction key to Panx1 ion selectivity (Figure 3f).
evidence: This is an inference stated in the Results section based on structural data.

claim: Trp74Ala showed a marked decrease in Cl- permeability and an increase in Na+ permeability.
source: Trp74Ala showed a marked decrease in Cl- permeability and an increase in Na+ permeability, despite preservation of the positive charge at Arg75.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by electrophysiology data.

claim: Trp74Phe disrupted ion selectivity, suggesting that proper positioning of the benzene ring at position 74 is important for anion selection.
source: A more conservative mutation, Trp74Phe, still disrupted ion selectivity, suggesting that proper positioning of the benzene ring at position 74 is important for anion selection.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by electrophysiology data.

claim: Anion selectivity is only achieved when Trp74 and Arg75 form a cation-π interaction.
source: Altogether, our data suggests that anion selectivity is only achieved when Trp74 and Arg75 form a cation-π interaction.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on mutagenesis data.

claim: It is possible that additional ion selectivity or gating regions exist in the full-length channel.
source: Given that our structure has disordered and truncated regions in the N-terminus, ICL1, and ICL2, it is possible that additional ion selectivity or gating regions exist in the full-length channel.
evidence: This is a speculative statement in the Results section.

claim: The N-termini of LRRC8 and connexins perform an important role in ion selectivity.
source: For example, the N-termini of LRRC8 and connexins perform an important role in ion selectivity (Kyle et al., 2008; Kronengold et al., 2012; Kefauver et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations.

claim: It is possible that the N-terminus of Panx1 is mobile and may further constrict the permeation pathway.
source: It is possible that the N-terminus of Panx1 is mobile and may further constrict the permeation pathway.
evidence: This is a speculative statement in the Results section.

claim: The electrostatic potential along the pore pathway may contribute to the ion selectivity.
source: Another possibility is that the electrostatic potential along the pore pathway contributes to the ion selectivity.
evidence: This is a speculative statement in the Results section.

claim: Both cytoplasmic and extracellular entrances of the permeation pathway are mostly basic.
source: Interestingly, both cytoplasmic and extracellular entrances of the permeation pathway are mostly basic, suggesting that non-permeant cations may be excluded from the pore (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by electrostatic potential calculations.

claim: Non-permeant cations may be excluded from the pore due to the basic nature of the entrances.
source: Interestingly, both cytoplasmic and extracellular entrances of the permeation pathway are mostly basic, suggesting that non-permeant cations may be excluded from the pore (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an inference stated in the Results section based on electrostatic potential data.

claim: The region underneath the W74 constriction is highly acidic.
source: In contrast, the region underneath the W74 constriction is highly acidic, supporting the idea that anions may be selected around this area.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by electrostatic potential data.

claim: Anions may be selected around the region underneath the W74 constriction.
source: In contrast, the region underneath the W74 constriction is highly acidic, supporting the idea that anions may be selected around this area.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the Results section based on electrostatic potential data.

claim: CBX likely acts through a mechanism involving ECL1.
source: We have previously demonstrated that CBX, a potent nonselective inhibitor of Panx1, likely acts through a mechanism involving ECL1 (Michalski and Kawate, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Mutations at a number of residues in ECL1 rendered Panx1 less sensitive to CBX-mediated channel inhibition.
source: In these experiments, mutations at a number of residues in ECL1 rendered Panx1 less sensitive to CBX-mediated channel inhibition.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Residues that affect CBX sensitivity are clustered proximal to the extracellular constriction by Trp74, in a groove formed between ECL1 and ECL2.
source: Mapping such residues in the Panx1 structure revealed that they are clustered proximal to the extracellular constriction by Trp74, in a groove formed between ECL1 and ECL2 (Figure 4a and b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural mapping.

claim: CBX is an allosteric inhibitor, not a channel blocker.
source: This supports our previous speculation that CBX is an allosteric inhibitor, not a channel blocker (Michalski and Kawate, 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by structural data and a citation.

claim: Mutations at Ile247, Val258, and Phe262 (hPanx1 numbering) in ECL2 diminished CBX-sensitivity.
source: We found that mutations at Ile247, Val258, and Phe262 (hPanx1 numbering) diminished CBX-sensitivity (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by electrophysiology data.

claim: Both ECL1 and ECL2 play important roles in inhibition of Panx1 by CBX.
source: These data suggest that both ECL1 and ECL2 play important roles in inhibition of Panx1 by CBX.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Results section based on mutagenesis data.

claim: CBX inhibits Panx channels by binding between ECL1 and ECL2 and 'locking' the conformation of gate forming ECL1 in favor of channel closure.
source: Although we do not have a cryo-EM structure complexed to CBX at this point, we speculate that CBX inhibits Panx channels by binding between ECL1 and ECL2 and 'locking' the conformation of gate forming ECL1 in favor of channel closure.
evidence: This is a speculative statement in the Results section based on structural and functional data.

claim: The frPanx1-ΔLC structure uncovered a unique heptameric assembly of a large-pore channel that harbors an extracellular constriction formed by Trp74 and Arg75.
source: The frPanx1-ΔLC structure uncovered a unique heptameric assembly of a large-pore channel that harbors an extracellular constriction formed by Trp74 and Arg75.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of findings.

claim: Trp74 and Arg75 are located on ECL1 and face toward the central pore of the channel.
source: These residues are located on ECL1 and face toward the central pore of the channel and thus, are situated to regulate channel function.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by structural data.

claim: Trp74 and Arg75 play pivotal roles in ion selection.
source: Mutagenesis studies at these positions revealed that both residues play pivotal roles in ion selection.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by mutagenesis data.

claim: The positively charged Arg75 does not seem to form a canonical selectivity filter.
source: Unlike the LRRC8A anion channel, however, the positively charged Arg75 does not seem to form a canonical selectivity filter.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the data.

claim: The guanidino group of Arg75 likely mediates a cation-π interaction with Trp74 in the neighboring subunit, which seems to control ion selection.
source: Instead, the guanidino group of Arg75 likely mediates a cation-π interaction with Trp74 in the neighboring subunit, which seems to control ion selection.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of structural and functional data.

claim: One possible ion selection mechanism is that the cation-π interaction stabilizes the inter-subunit interactions, which in turn creates an electrostatic environment that favors anion permeation.
source: One possible ion selection mechanism is that this cation-π interaction stabilizes the inter-subunit interactions, which in turn creates an electrostatic environment that favors anion permeation.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed in the Discussion section.

claim: Another possibility is that tight inter-subunit interactions in the extracellular domain are necessary to form an ion selectivity filter in the missing region in the current model (e.g. N-terminus or C-terminal domain).
source: Another possibility is that tight inter-subunit interactions in the extracellular domain are necessary to form an ion selectivity filter in the missing region in our current model (e.g. N-terminus or C-terminal domain).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed in the Discussion section.

claim: The current structure may represent a closed conformation based on the lack of channel activity at 0 mV.
source: Based on the lack of channel activity at 0 mV (Figure 1—figure supplement 2e and f), our current structure may represent a closed conformation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation stated in the Discussion section based on electrophysiology data.

claim: The existence of a highly acidic region near Trp74 may serve as a barrier for anions to permeate, supporting the closed conformation hypothesis.
source: This is supported by the existence of a highly acidic region near Trp74 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), which may serve as a barrier for anions to permeate.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as support for the closed conformation hypothesis.

claim: Given that the narrowest constriction at Trp74 is ~10 Å wide, it is possible that the structure actually represents an open conformation.
source: However, given that the narrowest constriction at Trp74 is ~10 Å wide, it is possible that the structure actually represents an open conformation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement in the Discussion section based on structural measurements.

claim: The +GS version of frPanx1-ΔLC shows larger leak currents, suggesting that the C-terminal truncation may promote channel opening while lack of the N-terminal modification renders it closed.
source: Indeed, the +GS version of frPanx1-ΔLC shows larger leak currents (Figure 1a and b), suggesting that the C-terminal truncation may promote channel opening while lack of the N-terminal modification renders it closed.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by electrophysiology data.

claim: If the conformation of the N-terminus in frPanx1-ΔLC is somehow compromised during purification or reconstitution into nanodiscs, it is possible that the structure may actually look closer to the +GS version.
source: If the conformation of the N-terminus in frPanx1-ΔLC is somehow compromised during purification or reconstitution into nanodiscs, it is possible that our structure may actually look closer to the +GS version.
evidence: This is a speculative statement in the Discussion section.

claim: The weak EM density in the N-terminal region leaves the possibility that frPanx1-ΔLC may be representing an open state.
source: While further studies are necessary to define the functional state of our current structure, the weak EM density in the N-terminal region leaves the possibility that frPanx1-ΔLC may be representing an open state.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a possibility based on structural data.

claim: ECL1 and ECL2 interact with each other and form a potential CBX binding pocket.
source: We found that ECL1 and ECL2 interact to each other and form a potential CBX binding pocket.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by structural data.

claim: Both ECL1 and ECL2 may undergo movement based on conformational alterations of the TMDs and cytoplasmic domains.
source: Both ECL1 and ECL2 may undergo movement based on conformational alterations of the TMDs and cytoplasmic domains.
evidence: This is a speculative statement in the Discussion section.

claim: Movement of the TMDs caused by membrane stretch or voltage, or changes in the cytoplasmic domain triggered by caspase cleavage may be coupled to conformational rearrangements in the extracellular domain.
source: For example, it is conceivable that movement of the TMDs caused by membrane stretch or voltage, or changes in the cytoplasmic domain triggered by caspase cleavage may be coupled to conformational rearrangements in the extracellular domain.
evidence: This is a speculative statement in the Discussion section.

claim: The major role of the extracellular domain in pannexin function is strongly supported by experimental results demonstrating that mutating Trp74 and Arg75, as well as surrounding residues in ECL1 and ECL2, alter channel properties including ion selectivity.
source: The major role of the extracellular domain in pannexin function is strongly supported by our experimental results demonstrating that mutating Trp74 and Arg75, as well as surrounding residues in ECL1 and ECL2, alter channel properties including ion selectivity.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by mutagenesis data.

claim: Application of CBX to mutants at Trp74 (e.g. to Ala, Ile, Lys) potentiates voltage-dependent channel activity.
source: Furthermore, we previously demonstrated that application of CBX to mutants at Trp74 (e.g. to Ala, Ile, Lys) potentiates voltage-dependent channel activity (Michalski and Kawate, 2016), which indicates that CBX likely acts as an allosteric inhibitor rather than a channel blocker.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: CBX likely acts as an allosteric inhibitor rather than a channel blocker.
source: Furthermore, we previously demonstrated that application of CBX to mutants at Trp74 (e.g. to Ala, Ile, Lys) potentiates voltage-dependent channel activity (Michalski and Kawate, 2016), which indicates that CBX likely acts as an allosteric inhibitor rather than a channel blocker.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by experimental evidence and citation.

claim: Roles of the intracellular domain remain elusive.
source: In contrast to the extracellular domain, roles of the intracellular domain remain elusive.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The C-terminal domain has been demonstrated to play important roles in Panx1 channel gating.
source: While the C-terminal domain has been demonstrated to play important roles in Panx1 channel gating (Sandilos et al., 2012), our study neither confirms or refutes this mechanism as half of this domain is missing in our current structure.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation.

claim: The first 10 residues in the N-terminus are disordered, making it challenging to understand how these residues tune the activity of Panx1 channel.
source: Likewise, the first 10 residues in the N-terminus are disordered, making it challenging to understand how these residues tune the activity of Panx1 channel (Michalski et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by structural data and a citation.

claim: It is possible that the unmodeled N-terminal region may interact with the deleted region of the C-terminal domain.
source: Given their important roles in channel gating, it is possible that the unmodeled N-terminal region may interact with the deleted region of the C-terminal domain.
evidence: This is a speculative statement in the Discussion section.

claim: It is possible that the N-terminal and C-terminal domains may form a channel gate.
source: It is also possible that these domains may form a channel gate.
evidence: This is a speculative statement in the Discussion section.

claim: The deleted residues in ICL-1 (between Gly171 and Lys194) seem to play a minimal role in channel gating.
source: In contrast to these domains, the deleted residues in ICL-1 (between Gly171 and Lys194) seems to play a minimal role in channel gating.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by experimental data.

claim: All deletion constructs in ICL-1 showed voltage-dependent channel activity via whole-cell patch clamp, with the exception of a construct in which the entire region between Lys155 and Lys194 was removed.
source: We surveyed 23 different deletion constructs (in which each variant harbored a different deletion length and position) and among these, all deletions constructs showed voltage-dependent channel activity via whole-cell patch clamp, with the exception of a construct in which the entire region between Lys155 and Lys194 was removed.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and describes experimental results.

claim: All functional ICL-1 deletion constructs were properly assembled into heptamers.
source: We also tested these deletion constructs using FSEC and found that all functional constructs were properly assembled into heptamers.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and describes experimental results.

claim: The deleted region in ILC-1 plays an insignificant role in channel gating.
source: The above evidence indicates that the deleted region in ILC-1 plays an insignificant role in channel gating.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion section based on experimental data.

claim: The EM density in the ICL-1 region was weak and could not be modeled, indicating a high degree of conformational flexibility.
source: The EM density in this region was weak and could not be modeled, indicating a high degree of conformational flexibility.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and describes the cryo-EM data.

claim: The frPanx1-ΔLC structure provides an important atomic blueprint for dissecting functional mechanisms of Panx1.
source: In conclusion, our frPanx1-ΔLC structure provides an important atomic blueprint for dissecting functional mechanisms of Panx1.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the significance of the work.

claim: The missing domains, especially the N-terminal loop and the C-terminal domain, may serve as a channel gate on the intracellular side of the channel.
source: While we did not observe a gate-like structure in the current cryo-EM map, the missing domains, especially the N-terminal loop and the C-terminal domain, may serve as a channel gate on the intracellular side of the channel.
evidence: This is a speculative statement in the Discussion section.
